discovery: Laser-driven plasma wakefield acceleration of electrons
motivation: In 1979 Tajima (with the late John Dawson) showed theoretically that an intense laser pulse traversing an underdense plasma excites a wake whose longitudinal electric field can exceed conventional accelerator gradients by three orders of magnitude. This was a remarkable piece of plasma-wave theory with a clear, testable prediction. Malka and Leemans led the experiments that realised it: in 2004 their groups, among others, produced quasi-monoenergetic electron beams from centimetre-scale plasmas, and Leemans' team later reached multi-GeV energies with guided laser channels. Laser wakefield acceleration now drives compact X-ray sources, free-electron-laser demonstrations and studies of radiation reaction and strong-field QED in laser-electron collisions. It turns collective plasma nonlinearity into a controllable tool and opens extreme regimes of light-matter interaction to laboratory study.
